spot-the-shift.title: Spot the shift
spot-the-shift.intro: Some objects change position between observations. Can you find one?

steps.title: Step through the dates
steps.prompt: Use the timeline or press play. Watch the stars between dates.
steps.done: Nice. Most stars stay put, which is what makes movers stand out.

steps.title: Click what moved
steps.prompt: Click the object you think changed position. (Candidate markers are hidden for this step.)
hints: Look for a bright dot that is not in the same place on every date.
It is in the lower-left part of the field on the earliest date.
It moves up and to the right as the dates advance.
steps.correct: Yes, that is the one. Candidate SX-0017 shifts between dates.
steps.incorrect: Not quite. That source stays put. Try another, or ask for a hint.

steps.title: Confirm with a blink comparison
steps.prompt: Open Compare, pick two dates and blink them. Does the source jump?
steps.done: Blinking is a classic way to spot movement.

spot-the-shift.explanation: Sources that appear to move are candidates, not discoveries. Real confirmation needs alignment checks, uncertainty estimates and follow-up outside this app. All content here is illustrative.

investigate: Why does the score not mean probability?
compare: What does the difference image show?
What could cause a false difference?
spectrum: What do the error bars mean?

beginner: Infrared is light with a longer wavelength than your eyes can see. It passes through dust better than visible light, so it shows cooler and dustier things.
advanced: Near-infrared bands trace cool photospheres and warm dust. Broad spectral coverage lets one source be characterised across wavelength.
caveats: General background, not a finding about this data.

beginner: Proper motion is how far a star appears to drift across the sky each year. Nearby stars drift faster.
advanced: Proper motion is the angular rate of change of position on the sky, usually in arcsec per year. Catalogue values are shown separately from anything this app derives.
caveats: Catalogue values in this sample are quoted for illustration.

beginner: The score only ranks candidates. A higher number means the sample method found a clearer change. It does not mean 'more likely to be real'.
advanced: The ranking score is unitless and defined by its basis string. It is not a calibrated probability or confidence level.
caveats: Mock score. Real score semantics come from the backend (`scoreBasis`).

beginner: It is listed because something about it changes between dates. Check the evidence list under the candidates panel to see what.
advanced: Candidates are listed by the backend from positional or brightness change between aligned observations. The evidence and warnings fields explain each one.
caveats: A candidate is not a confirmed object.

beginner: A difference image can light up for real changes, but also for noise, small alignment errors, or differences in how the images were calibrated.
advanced: Residuals can arise from registration error, resampling, PSF or calibration differences between epochs, and noise. Check the compatibility checks and the stated uncertainty.
caveats: A difference alone is not evidence of real change.

beginner: Two observations are comparable if they cover similar wavelengths, overlap on the sky and were calibrated the same way. The Compare page lists each check.
advanced: The backend gates comparison on footprint, wavelength overlap at the position, calibration, alignment residual, quality and data release. `notEvaluated` is not a pass.

beginner: A spectrum shows how bright something is at different infrared colours. Missing bands are gaps where no usable observation exists. Error bars appear only when an uncertainty is available.
advanced: The spectrum is assembled from several observations, so points can come from different dates. Gaps are not interpolated; error bars are drawn only where the backend supplied an uncertainty.
caveats: Illustrative synthetic spectrum, not a SPHEREx measurement.

beginner: Here is a short recap of your investigation: you picked a target, looked at observations over time, and may have added notes. Keep going by comparing two dates.
advanced: Summary (mock): target selected, observations reviewed, notes and bookmarks recorded. No result here is a confirmed detection.
caveats: Mock summary generated without an LLM.

params.text: Reviewed observations; next: compare two dates.

beginner: Try pressing play to blink through the dates. Then click a candidate to see why it is listed.
advanced: Select a candidate, review its evidence and warnings, then run a difference comparison between the dates either side of the change.

beginner: You are looking at a sample sky image of your selected target on one date. The circles mark candidates that seem to change.
advanced: A display raster of one observation with candidate markers. The viewer applies no scientific processing. Brightness and contrast are cosmetic.
caveats: Image is procedurally generated for this demo.

beginner: I can explain infrared light, candidates, comparisons and spectra. Try one of the suggested questions.
advanced: No scripted answer matched. Try asking about candidates, comparisons, uncertainty, proper motion or spectra.
